prompt: At peak, 1,300/s arrive. Your app server can serve 200/s and your database 300/s, and each request makes one database query. How many requests per second complete the whole path?

options.whyWrong: This counts every arriving request as completed. Load past a component’s capacity is dropped, so a path can’t complete more than its narrowest hop.
This adds the two capacities as if a request could use either one. Each request crosses both hops in turn, so capacities don’t add along a path.
This is the larger of the two capacities. A request has to cross both hops, so the smaller one sets the limit.

explanation: A request completes only if every hop serves it. The app server serves 200/s and passes those on; the database serves 200/s of them. So the path completes 200/s: never more than its narrowest hop, whatever the other can do.

prompt: An app server takes 50 ms to serve a request with nothing queued, and its capacity is 60/s. At peak, 30/s arrive. How many requests per second does it complete?

explanation: It completes all 30/s: the load is under its 60/s capacity, so nothing is dropped. The 50 ms service time says how long each request takes, not how many the server can take, because it works on many at once.

prompt: A component that can serve 300/s receives 750/s at peak. In this game, what share of the requests it receives fail?

options.whyWrong: This divides the dropped load by capacity. The error rate is a share of the requests that arrived, so it divides by what was received.
This is the share of requests that succeed, not the share that fail. The two add up to 100%.
This assumes load past capacity waits its turn and eventually succeeds. Past capacity a queue only grows; this game turns the excess away at once, and those requests fail.

explanation: It serves 300/s and drops the other 450/s. The error rate is dropped ÷ received: 450 ÷ 750 = 60%. Dividing by capacity instead overstates it, because the failures are a share of the requests that arrived.

options.whyWrong: This divides the dropped load by capacity. The error rate is a share of the requests that arrived, so it divides by what was received.
This assumes load past capacity waits its turn and eventually succeeds. Past capacity a queue only grows; this game turns the excess away at once, and those requests fail.
